title: Understanding P-Trap Blockages in Kitchen Sinks
description: An educational breakdown showing how fats, oils, grease (FOG), and un-dissolved food debris settle inside the curve of a P-trap, leading to slow drainage and persistent sink blockages.
image_prompt: A clean, photorealistic educational technical visualization of the under-sink area of a modern kitchen sink in a vertical 9:16 aspect ratio. Centered in the frame is a white PVC tubular P-trap connected correctly to a stainless steel sink tailpiece above and leading into a wall drain stub-out behind it. A detailed cross-section cutaway view of the P-trap's lower curved bend reveals the internal mechanism: standing liquid water seal with visible, physically realistic accumulation of cooled, solidified grease and organic food debris clinging along the lower wall of the pipe bend, narrowing the flow path. Realistic under-cabinet lighting illuminates the white PVC fittings, brass slip-nuts, and grey wall background. Clean visual space at the top third and bottom third for text overlays. High resolution, clear technical visual focus. No text, no labels, no arrows, no diagrams, no watermarks, no logos, no brand labels.
visual_story: The visual highlights a realistic under-sink drainage setup with a cutaway view of the P-trap bend. Viewers can see how the standing water seal—which normally prevents sewer gases from entering the room—also acts as a cooling basin where warm liquid grease cools down and solidifies at the lowest point. By illustrating the constricted pipe interior, the visual directly links daily kitchen habits to physical flow restriction.

on_image_text.hook: Why Kitchen Sinks Block at the Curve
on_image_text.explanation: Standing water in the P-trap cools warm grease, causing it to solidify along the pipe bend.
on_image_text.callout: FOG & Solid Scrap Buildup in P-Trap
on_image_text.takeaway: Scrape plates and wipe greasy pans into the trash before washing.
